title: I gave AI agents deploy keys to my paper desks. They deployed 781 bots, backtested 8 of them first, and are down $1.34M. The control that mattered was not a prompt.
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Robinhood's number this week was 50,000 accounts where an AI trades for you. Mine is smaller and worse. I gave AI agents deploy keys to paper desks on the trading lab I built, and pulled the audit log this afternoon to see what they did with them.

781 bots deployed through agent keys, on 16 desks, between Aug 19 and Aug 24. 727 are still running. 18,845 closed paper trades, 8,992 winners, realised −$1,335,857. 101 of the 781 have never placed a trade at all.

The number that actually bothered me: 773 of the 781 were deployed without being backtested first. The engine grades on request and never grades behind your back, so the agents just skipped it. Eight got a verdict. Four of those were SHELF, meaning "don't run this", and they ran anyway. The engine advises, the deployer decides, and the deployer was a language model with a deploy scope.

The worst bot is a put buyer on TSLA/AMD/META/NFLX, 53 trades, −$145,438. The best is a call buyer on SPY/AAPL/NVDA/TSLA, 8 trades, +$24,392. Same kind of strategy, same author, opposite result. That's the sample size talking, not the AI.

The control that mattered was not a prompt. When you make a key it opens exactly one desk. It gets a scope: read only, backtest only, or allowed to deploy. And there's a kill switch that pauses every agent at once. The agent can read whether it's frozen. There is deliberately no tool to unfreeze. Only a signed-in human can flip it back, so an agent can never let itself out.

Two honest footnotes. Of the 33 keys ever minted, 0 were given the safe backtest-only default, mine included, everyone picks deploy. And the kill switch has been thrown exactly 0 times, because it's all paper money and I keep telling myself that's fine.

I built this. It's free to start. Happy to answer anything about the mechanics.

comments.author: NefariousnessOpening
comments.body: i have seen several reports about this and they are are losses. the premise is all bad. backtesting can just as easily (likely will) make the model internalize data that make it worse. the system has been described enough times now that i can read with conviction there are not enough pieces for the game they are selling. the system is not finished and they are selling it.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Nothing's being sold. It's free and every dollar in that post is paper. Not finished is right, that's why the losses are the headline and not a pitch. If backtesting made the agents worse I'd want to see it, 773 of the 781 skipped it entirely.

replies.author: NefariousnessOpening
replies.body: i know what paper trading is. the point of it is supposed to be to get your strategy sorted without the risk. i assumed it would work very well never questioned it. eventually i learned why it can also be bad

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: It goes bad when the fills are fantasy. Ours buy at the ask and sell at the bid, which is why the fleet shows a 1.3M paper loss instead of a flattering one. The ugly number is the point of it.

comments.author: ozgqr
comments.body: the deploy-scope split is the real finding here. i’d make `backtest_only` the only mintable default, then require a verdict bound to the exact strategy hash and data window before issuing a deploy capability; otherwise an agent can backtest one artifact and deploy a changed one. the signed human-only unfreeze is the right asymmetry too. Marx would be useful only if its investigation record carried that same strategy hash, so later results cannot be detached from what actually ran.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: backtest_only as the only mintable default is the first change I'd make. right now the owner picks scopes at mint and 12 of the 22 live keys carry deploy. the hash binding isn't built at all: deploy takes a strategy id and the strategy can be edited after grading. that's the hole. hash at grade, compare at deploy, refuse on mismatch.

comments.author: ConfidentAction1548
comments.body: 773 out of 781 skipping the backtest is honestly the most interesting part here. Feels like the guardrail has to live outside the agent rather than relying on the model to decide when it’s ready. I do something similar manually with Moon’s play money side when I’m testing directional ideas so real money doesn’t enter the equation until the idea has survived a separate testing stage.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: outside the agent is where it's going. today the key scope is the only gate and 12 of the 22 live keys carry deploy from day one. the change on the table is backtest-only as the sole mintable default, deploy added by the owner by hand. does moon's play-money side gate on anything, or is it just a separate wallet?

replies.author: ConfidentAction1548
replies.body: Its basically a separate simulated balance rather than a permissions gate like the key scopes youre describing. I use it for testing trades without touching real funds but I wouldnt treat it as equivalent to making deploy a separately granted permission.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: A sandbox answers which money, a scope answers which verb. Ours has both, and the verb half is the weak one: 12 of the 22 live keys got deploy at mint because that was the default. Backtest-only default, deploy added by hand, is where I'm leaning. Would you let an agent hold deploy at all, or keep that owner-only forever?
